title: Carbonate model and reference sheet
text:
Species and equilibria
Write \(\mathrm{CO_2^*}\) for \(\mathrm{CO_2(aq)}+\mathrm{H_2CO_3}\). It is a combined pool, not the chemical formula of a single molecule. Most of this pool is dissolved molecular carbon dioxide under these conditions. The effective first dissociation incorporates hydration:
\[\mathrm{CO_2^* + H_2O \rightleftharpoons H^+ + HCO_3^-},\qquad
K_1=10^{-6.35}.\]
\[\mathrm{HCO_3^- \rightleftharpoons H^+ + CO_3^{2-}},\qquad
K_2=10^{-10.33}.\]
In the first expression, the water term represents the net reaction of dissolved carbon dioxide; the notation groups hydrated and unhydrated forms together.
The total dissolved inorganic carbon in this model is
\[C_T=[\mathrm{CO_2^*}]+[\mathrm{HCO_3^-}]+[\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}].\]
No carbon leaves this sum merely because it changes species. Mineral reactions, gas exchange, or biological transformations can change the dissolved total.

title: Carbonate model and reference sheet
section: Ratios and fractions at a supplied pH
text:
Ratios and fractions at a supplied pH
Dividing the equilibrium expressions gives
\[r_1=\frac{[\mathrm{HCO_3^-}]}{[\mathrm{CO_2^*}]}=
10^{\mathrm{pH}-6.35},\qquad
r_2=\frac{[\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}]}{[\mathrm{HCO_3^-}]}=
10^{\mathrm{pH}-10.33}.\]
The proportions of the three species are \(1:r_1:r_1r_2\). Therefore
\[\alpha_0=\frac{1}{1+r_1+r_1r_2},\quad
\alpha_1=\frac{r_1}{1+r_1+r_1r_2},\quad
\alpha_2=\frac{r_1r_2}{1+r_1+r_1r_2}.\]
Each \(\alpha\) is dimensionless and each concentration is \(\alpha_i C_T\). The fractions sum to one. In this model the fractions depend on pH and the constants; \(C_T\) sets the concentration scale. A distribution curve supplies possible compositions at prescribed pH values. It does not solve for pH.

title: Carbonate model and reference sheet
text:
Alkalinity and buffering
The carbonate-only total alkalinity is
\[A_T=[\mathrm{HCO_3^-}]+2[\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}]
+[\mathrm{OH^-}]-[\mathrm{H^+}],\qquad
[\mathrm{OH^-}]=K_w/[\mathrm{H^+}].\]
Use mol of charge equivalents per litre (eq/L); \(1\) meq/L is \(10^{-3}\) eq/L. Bicarbonate contributes one equivalent per mole, carbonate two. Real freshwater can have additional alkalinity contributions, so this expression must be checked before applying it to measurements. The USGS carbonate-speciation guidance explains the importance of other acid-neutralising species.
Alkalinity describes an acid-neutralising balance relative to the carbon dioxide reference state. pH describes hydrogen-ion activity at the present state. Local buffer capacity describes the amount of acid or base required for a small pH change under specified conditions. These are related, but are different quantities.
For a strong-acid addition \(q\) eq/L with negligible dilution and no other reaction, \(A_{T,\mathrm{after}}=A_{T,\mathrm{before}}-q\). In a closed water with no mineral or biological reactions, \(C_T\) stays constant. Added acid redistributes carbon toward \(\mathrm{CO_2^*}\). The final pH must satisfy both the carbon balance and the new alkalinity.

title: Carbonate model and reference sheet
text:
Gas and mineral boundaries
For water equilibrated with a large gas reservoir, use the specified convention
\[[\mathrm{CO_2^*}]=K_H p_{\mathrm{CO_2}}.\]
Here partial pressure is in atm. Applying this coefficient to total inorganic carbon would be incorrect. Gas uptake by itself changes \(C_T\) but conserves \(A_T\) in our model. At fixed alkalinity it generally lowers pH. Fixing gas pressure, pH, and \(C_T\) independently would usually overconstrain the model.
For calcite, \(\mathrm{CaCO_3(s)\rightleftharpoons Ca^{2+}+CO_3^{2-}}\). Use the free-ion concentrations to estimate
\[\Omega=\frac{[\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}][\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}]}{K_{sp}}.\]
\(\Omega<1\) indicates undersaturation; dissolution is thermodynamically favoured if calcite is available. \(\Omega>1\) indicates supersaturation; precipitation can be favoured, but kinetics and nucleation can delay it. \(\Omega=1\) is saturation. Dissolving one mole of calcite adds one mole to dissolved inorganic carbon and two equivalents to alkalinity. This process is excluded from the closed acid example.

title: Carbonate species and alkalinity
text:
Same pH, different response
Two constructed waters start at pH 7.50.

Water A: total dissolved inorganic carbon = 1.00 mmol/L.
Water B: total dissolved inorganic carbon = 0.100 mmol/L.
Each receives 0.050 mmol/L of strong acid, with negligible dilution.

Which water changes more? What does pH alone leave out?

This is a closed-water thought experiment: no gas exchange, minerals, biological carbon transformations, or noncarbonate buffers. Background counterions provide electroneutrality; this is not a recipe for preparing a solution from CO2 alone.

title: Carbonate species and alkalinity
text:
Three questions for this lecture

Which dissolved carbon species dominate at a given pH?
How do species fractions differ from concentrations?
Why do pH and alkalinity describe different aspects of water?

Use 25 °C and the dilute freshwater approximation throughout.

title: Carbonate species and alkalinity
text:
One element, three dissolved pools
C_T=[\mathrm{CO_2^*}]+[\mathrm{HCO_3^-}]+[\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}]
\mathrm{CO_2^*} groups dissolved carbon dioxide and carbonic acid.
Changing species redistributes carbon. It does not itself remove dissolved carbon.

title: Carbonate species and alkalinity
text:
Carbonate reactions release hydrogen ions
\mathrm{CO_2^*+H_2O\rightleftharpoons H^++HCO_3^-} \mathrm{HCO_3^-\rightleftharpoons H^++CO_3^{2-}}
Use effective pK_1=6.35 and pK_2=10.33.
Adding acid shifts both equilibria toward the left.

CO2* is a combined analytical pool. The first displayed reaction is shorthand for dissolution/hydration followed by acid dissociation, not an elementary reaction. All constants and the model definition are on the reference sheet.

title: Carbonate species and alkalinity
section: From an equilibrium expression to a ratio
text:
From an equilibrium expression to a ratio
K_1=\frac{[\mathrm{H^+}][\mathrm{HCO_3^-}]}{[\mathrm{CO_2^*}]}
Since [\mathrm{H^+}]\approx10^{-\mathrm{pH}} mol/L,
\frac{[\mathrm{HCO_3^-}]}{[\mathrm{CO_2^*}]}=10^{\mathrm{pH}-6.35}.
At pH 7.35 the ratio is 10. At pH 6.35 it is 1.

title: Carbonate species and alkalinity
text:
Include the second dissociation
r_1=10^{\mathrm{pH}-6.35},\qquad r_2=10^{\mathrm{pH}-10.33}
The three proportions are 1:r_1:r_1r_2.
At pH 8.35 they are approximately 1:100:1.047.
Divide each by their sum to obtain fractions: 0.00980, 0.97994, 0.01026.

title: Carbonate species and alkalinity
text:
Read the distribution diagram



Model species fractions at prescribed pH values, 25 °C.


Which species dominates near pH 8? Where do adjacent fractions cross?

At each pKa the corresponding adjacent species are equal. Neither is exactly half of all carbon because the third species still exists. The horizontal axis is supplied pH, not acid dose or elapsed time.

title: Carbonate species and alkalinity
section: Fractions do not give the amount
text:
Fractions do not give the amount
At pH 8.35, bicarbonate is about 0.980 of C_T.

If C_T=1.00 mmol/L, bicarbonate is about 0.980 mmol/L.
If C_T=0.100 mmol/L, bicarbonate is about 0.0980 mmol/L.

The fraction is the same. The acid-neutralising inventories differ.

title: Carbonate species and alkalinity
text:
Alkalinity counts charge equivalents
A_T=[\mathrm{HCO_3^-}]+2[\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}]
+[\mathrm{OH^-}]-[\mathrm{H^+}]
One mole of bicarbonate contributes one equivalent; carbonate contributes two.
pH describes the current hydrogen-ion activity. Alkalinity describes an acid-neutralising balance. Buffer capacity describes resistance to a small pH change.

title: Carbonate species and alkalinity
text:
Acid changes the balance
\mathrm{HCO_3^-+H^+\rightarrow CO_2^*+H_2O}
For a strong-acid input q eq/L:
A_{T,\mathrm{after}}=A_{T,\mathrm{before}}-q.
In our closed example C_T stays fixed. pH must adjust to the new balance. Do not subtract an acid dose directly from a pH value.

title: Carbonate chemistry exercises
text: Use the model sheet throughout: 25 °C, dilute freshwater, \(pK_1=6.35\), \(pK_2=10.33\), and the supplied Henry and calcite constants. All waters and gas inputs below are constructed teaching examples.

title: Carbonate chemistry exercises
section: 1. Predict, then calculate a species distribution
text:
1. Predict, then calculate a species distribution
A water has pH 8.35 and \(C_T=1.00\) mmol/L.

Predict which of the three carbonate pools is largest.
Calculate \(r_1\) and \(r_2\), then the fractions of all three pools.
Calculate their concentrations in mmol/L and check the carbon balance.
Repeat only the concentration step for \(C_T=0.100\) mmol/L at the same pH. Explain what changed and what did not.







Hint





The proportions are \(1:r_1:r_1r_2\), so divide each by their sum. The ratio \(r_2\) compares carbonate with bicarbonate; it is not the carbonate fraction.









Worked solution





At pH 8.35, \(r_1=100\) and \(r_2=10^{-1.98}=0.0104713\). The sum of the proportions is \(102.0471\).

The concentrations sum to 1.00 mmol/L within rounding. Bicarbonate dominates. For 0.100 mmol/L total, each concentration is one tenth as large; the fractions are unchanged. This result uses the same pH and dilute-solution constants.

title: Carbonate chemistry exercises
text:
2. Same pH, different acid response
Two constructed waters start at pH 7.50. Water A has \(C_T=1.00\) mmol/L; water B has \(C_T=0.100\) mmol/L. At this pH the fractions are \(\alpha_0=0.066023\), \(\alpha_1=0.932598\), \(\alpha_2=0.001379\).

Calculate initial alkalinity from the carbonate-only expression. Include water ions: \([\mathrm{H^+}]=3.1623\times10^{-8}\) mol/L and \([\mathrm{OH^-}]=3.1623\times10^{-7}\) mol/L.
Add 0.0500 mmol/L of a strong monoprotic acid to each, with negligible dilution. Calculate each new alkalinity. No gas exchange, mineral reaction, or biological transformation occurs. What happens to \(C_T\)?
A calculation satisfying both balances gives final pH values 7.235 for A and 6.252 for B. Explain the difference without assuming initial pH measures the acid-neutralising inventory.
Can you obtain the final pH by subtracting 0.0500 from 7.50? Explain the units.







Hint





First put all concentrations in mol/L. Multiply the carbonate concentration by two in the alkalinity expression. A mole of monoprotic strong acid supplies one equivalent. To express eq/L as meq/L, multiply by 1000.









Worked solution





For A, the bicarbonate and carbonate contribution is \((0.932598+2\times0.001379)\times10^{-3}\) eq/L. The water-ion term is \(2.8461\times10^{-7}\) eq/L. The resulting initial alkalinities are approximately 0.9356 meq/L for A and 0.09382 meq/L for B.
The acid supplies 0.0500 meq/L. Final alkalinities are therefore 0.8856 and 0.04382 meq/L. Carbon stays dissolved in this closed model, so each \(C_T\) is conserved; a larger fraction becomes CO₂*.
B loses about 53% of its initial alkalinity, compared with about 5.3% for A. Its larger pH fall is consistent with its smaller carbonate inventory. Alkalinity is not identical to local buffer capacity, but here the two waters have the same initial species fractions and different carbon amounts.
A pH difference is logarithmic and dimensionless; an acid dose has amount-per-volume units. Direct subtraction cannot satisfy the chemical balances. A numerical solver is not required for this exercise.

title: Carbonate chemistry exercises
section: 3. Use Henry’s law for the correct pool
text:
3. Use Henry’s law for the correct pool
A separate water equilibrates with a large gas reservoir having a supplied \(p_{\mathrm{CO_2}}=4.00\times10^{-4}\) atm. Use \(K_H=0.034\) mol L\(^{-1}\) atm\(^{-1}\).

Calculate \([\mathrm{CO_2^*}]\) and show the unit cancellation.
Is that enough information to calculate pH or \(C_T\)?
If the equilibrated water is also specified to have pH 8.35, calculate \(C_T\).
In another water, CO₂ enters while no acid, mineral, or biological process acts. Explain why the alkalinity stays constant even though pH can decrease.







Worked solution





\([\mathrm{CO_2^*}]=0.034\times4.00\times10^{-4}=1.36\times10^{-5}\) mol/L = 13.6 µmol/L. The atm units cancel. This specifies the gas pool only. Another independent carbonate constraint is needed to calculate pH and total carbon.
With pH 8.35 supplied, \(C_T=13.6(1+100+1.04713)\) µmol/L, or approximately 1.388 mmol/L. Henry’s law alone did not give that total.
Dissociation of the added CO₂ produces hydrogen ion and bicarbonate together; their contributions cancel in alkalinity. Gas transfer adds carbon rather than strong-acid equivalents. At fixed alkalinity the pH generally falls as CO₂ enters. An imposed pH of 8.35 is a specified state, not the predicted endpoint of every water exposed to this gas.

title: Carbonate chemistry exercises
text:
4. Check calcite saturation
Two separate water states each have free calcium \(5.00\times10^{-4}\) mol/L. Free carbonate is \(1.00\times10^{-6}\) mol/L in state X and \(1.00\times10^{-5}\) mol/L in state Y. Use \(K_{sp}=3.3\times10^{-9}\).
Calculate \(\Omega\) for each. Identify which could dissolve available calcite and which could precipitate it. Can you infer a precipitation rate or final mass? Explain why replacing free calcium with dissolved total calcium might matter.






Worked solution





The products are \(5.00\times10^{-10}\) and \(5.00\times10^{-9}\). Thus \(\Omega_X=0.152\) and \(\Omega_Y=1.52\). X is undersaturated and could dissolve calcite if it is present. Y is supersaturated, so precipitation is thermodynamically favoured, but may be delayed by kinetics or nucleation. Neither ratio gives a rate or final mass. Ion pairs and complexes can make free calcium smaller than total dissolved calcium.

title: Carbonate chemistry exercises
section: 5. Plot the chemical prediction in R
text:
5. Plot the chemical prediction in R
This task reuses objects, arithmetic, tables, and labelled plots from introductory computing. The small addition is a regular pH grid. No statistical fit is needed: these are predictions from equilibrium expressions.
Download speciation.R and report.Rmd into the same folder. Open that folder as your working project. The script needs ggplot2; rendering the report also needs rmarkdown, as in introductory computing. Open the script in the editor before running it.

Predict and inspect
Before running the script, sketch the expected dominance near pH 4, 8, and 12. The script starts with these calculations:
pH <- seq(4, 12, by = 0.05)
r1 <- 10^(pH - 6.35)
r2 <- 10^(pH - 10.33)
denominator <- 1 + r1 + r1 * r2
seq() creates regularly spaced values. Each vector operation evaluates the chemical expression at every pH value. ^ means a power. The script divides the three proportions by denominator and puts them in a table. Its remaining code arranges that table for the familiar ggplot() and geom_line() functions.
Run from the folder holding both files:
source("speciation.R")
head(speciation)
speciation_plot
Compare the plot with the prediction and with the hand calculation in question 1.



Three carbonate species fractions at prescribed pH, calculated from the supplied equilibrium model.




Check and explain

In the report template, select the pH 8.35 row and compare its fractions with your hand calculation. Explain any difference due to rounding.
Check that fractions stay between zero and one and sum to one.
Explain what happens to concentrations if \(C_T\) doubles at each prescribed pH.
Explain why moving along the horizontal axis does not simulate adding a specified dose of acid to a closed sample.
Replace the template prompts with your prediction, calculation, chemical interpretation, and assumptions. Restart R, then Knit the saved report, or run rmarkdown::render("report.Rmd") from its folder.







Worked interpretation





CO₂* dominates at low pH, bicarbonate in the middle, and carbonate at high pH. At pH 8.35, the model fractions agree with question 1. The sum is one to numerical precision, and every fraction lies between zero and one. Doubling \(C_T\) at fixed pH doubles the concentrations, while leaving these model fractions unchanged.
The horizontal axis supplies pH independently at each point. An acid-dose experiment must instead conserve carbon and satisfy the changed alkalinity. The curve alone does not supply that second constraint or predict a final pH. The model assumes equilibrium, 25 °C, and dilute freshwater; it omits ion pairing and other acid–base systems.

title: Carbonate chemistry exercises
text:
6. Explain a catchment observation
A lake’s pH decreases after a disturbance. Suggest two chemically distinct processes from this unit that could cause a decrease, and identify additional measurements that would help distinguish them. State one limitation of interpreting only pH. Do not claim a cause from a single observation.






Worked explanation





Strong-acid input and net CO₂ uptake can both lower pH. In the isolated model, strong acid lowers alkalinity while CO₂ uptake conserves it and increases dissolved inorganic carbon. Paired pH, alkalinity, and inorganic-carbon or dissolved-CO₂ measurements would help assess these possibilities. Calcium and mineral context could reveal additional reactions. A real catchment can have several processes acting together; pH alone does not identify the cause or neutralising inventory.

title: Environmental Chemistry
text:
How do chemical reactions determine what happens to a substance in air, water, and soil? We connect molecular properties, equilibria, reaction rates, and partitioning to environmental transport and exposure.






Note



The first teaching draft is available for carbonate and gas chemistry. The remaining topics are outlined for development.


The proposed sequence follows atmosphere, water, and the terrestrial environment, with particular attention to aquatic chemistry. See the content overview for the topics and chemical questions.
Calculations begin with a small worked example. Selected exercises then reuse R for tables, plots, and reproducible explanations of chemical results.
Start with carbonate and gas chemistry: short lectures, worked examples, exercises, and a species-distribution plot in R.

title: Proposed content overview
text: Follow a substance through environmental compartments. Practise concentration units, mass balances, and the distinction between equilibrium and reaction rate.

title: Proposed content overview
text:
Atmosphere
Explain ozone formation and removal, photochemical pollution, acid deposition, and the chemical roles of gases and particles in climate. Follow deposition into surface waters.

title: Proposed content overview
text:
Water
Use acid–base equilibria, carbonate buffering, and gas exchange to explain water composition. The first draft of carbonate and gas chemistry includes lectures and practice. Relate organic matter, redox conditions, metal complexation, and surface reactions to speciation and mobility. Apply these ideas to nutrient cycling and water treatment.

title: Proposed content overview
text:
Soils and contaminants
Explain retention and release in soils and sediments. Connect organic molecular properties to partitioning, persistence, and potential exposure. Use waste and leachate as applications of the same chemistry.

title: Proposed content overview
text:
Connecting the systems
Trace acid deposition through a catchment to a lake, or explain contaminant release when sediment conditions change. Support an explanation with reactions, a mass balance, and a clearly interpreted figure.

title: Proposed content overview
text:
Working reference
Gary W. vanLoon and Stephen J. Duffy, Environmental Chemistry: A Global Perspective, fourth edition, Oxford University Press, 2017, ISBN 9780198749974. Selected readings will follow the publisher’s chapter structure. This is the working reference for content development; assignment to this course is provisional.

title: Carbon dioxide exchange and carbonate minerals
section: What changes when the water meets air?
text:
What changes when the water meets air?
The closed acid example held dissolved inorganic carbon fixed.
Gas exchange allows carbon to enter or leave. Does it change alkalinity in the same way as strong acid?

title: Carbon dioxide exchange and carbonate minerals
text:
Specify the gas equilibrium convention
[\mathrm{CO_2^*}]=K_Hp_{\mathrm{CO_2}}
Here K_H=0.034 mol L^{-1} atm^{-1} at 25 °C.
Partial pressure in atm gives dissolved carbon dioxide in mol/L. A coefficient defined as pressure divided by concentration would require a different equation.

title: Carbon dioxide exchange and carbonate minerals
text:
A worked Henry calculation
Take a supplied gas pressure p_{\mathrm{CO_2}}=4.00\times10^{-4} atm.
[\mathrm{CO_2^*}]=0.034(4.00\times10^{-4})=
1.36\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{mol/L}=13.6\ \mathrm{\mu mol/L}.
This is the carbon dioxide pool, not total inorganic carbon. The gas pressure is an exercise input, not a claim about today’s atmosphere.

title: Carbon dioxide exchange and carbonate minerals
section: From the gas pool to total carbon
text:
From the gas pool to total carbon
If the equilibrated water is also specified to have pH 8.35,
C_T=[\mathrm{CO_2^*}](1+r_1+r_1r_2).
Using r_1=100 and r_2\approx0.01047:
C_T\approx13.6(102.047)=1388\ \mathrm{\mu mol/L}.
This describes a state with that pH and gas pressure. It does not predict the pH of arbitrary water exposed to the gas.

The statements exclude mineral reactions, biological transformations, and volume changes. CO2 creates H+ and bicarbonate together: their alkalinity contributions cancel. A finite headspace needs a gas-plus-water carbon balance rather than a fixed pressure assumption.

text:
Minerals introduce another reaction
\mathrm{CaCO_3(s)\rightleftharpoons Ca^{2+}+CO_3^{2-}}

The closed acid calculation excluded this possible source of neutralisation.

\Omega<1: undersaturated.
\Omega=1: saturated.

title: Carbon dioxide exchange and carbonate minerals
section: A field explanation needs the boundaries
text:
A field explanation needs the boundaries
A water can exchange gas, receive acid, dissolve minerals, and support biological carbon transformations at the same time.
Before calculating, identify which processes are included and what is fixed. Do not impose a fixed dissolved carbon total while also allowing unlimited gas exchange without a balancing constraint.

title: Carbon dioxide exchange and carbonate minerals
text:

Why can CO₂ uptake lower pH while conserving alkalinity?
Why can a mineral saturation calculation indicate a possible reaction without predicting its rate or final amount?
Work through the exercise. Constants, limitations, and sources are on the reference sheet.

title: Carbonate and gas chemistry
text:
Why can two waters with the same pH respond differently to an acid input? Carbonate equilibria connect dissolved carbon, acid neutralisation, gas exchange, and mineral stability. We will use a deliberately simple freshwater model to separate these effects.
Start with carbonate species and alkalinity, then gas exchange and minerals. Work through the exercises, including a short R activity. The model and reference sheet supplies all constants and assumptions. The reading context is chapters 10–11 of vanLoon and Duffy, fourth edition; precise subsection assignments remain to be selected.

title: Carbonate and gas chemistry
section: What you should be able to do
text:
What you should be able to do

Calculate carbonate species ratios at a supplied pH and interpret a distribution diagram.
Distinguish pH, total dissolved inorganic carbon, alkalinity, and buffer capacity.
Explain why a strong-acid input and carbon dioxide uptake change water differently.
Apply a specified Henry coefficient and a simple calcite saturation test.
Use a supplied R calculation to plot species fractions, check it against a hand calculation, and explain what the plot cannot predict.

title: Carbonate and gas chemistry
text:
Before starting
You need concentration units, an equilibrium expression, logarithms, and a balanced acid–base reaction. Recall that one millimole per litre is \(10^{-3}\) mol/L, and one micromole per litre is \(10^{-6}\) mol/L. Under our dilute-solution approximation, \(\mathrm{pH}=-\log_{10}[\mathrm{H^+}]\) when the numerical concentration is in mol/L. Thus pH 7 corresponds to \(10^{-7}\) mol/L, and lowering pH by one means ten times more hydrogen ion. The exact pH definition uses activity.
Try before reading further: does pH 8 tell you how many moles of acid a litre of water can neutralise? What additional information might you need?

title: Carbonate and gas chemistry

A catchment connection
Acid deposition can change the acid input to a lake. Catchment minerals, soil exchange, organic acids, and biological activity also influence the water. Here we isolate carbonate chemistry first. All numerical waters are constructed teaching examples, not measurements from a real lake. The gas-exchange examples are separate boundary conditions, not an assumed continuation of the closed-water acid experiment.
